articles.text: Negotiations with the teacher’s union have now lasted more than 365 days with more negotiations this week. After immense public pressure, including hundreds of lawn signs demanding a discussion about what will happen in the 2021-22 school year in the fall, the school board agreed to put that discussion on the table tonight, March 24, 2021. Plans for extending hours this spring and the 2021-22 school year just got easier thanks to health agencies revising the minimum distance between student desks from 6 feet down to 3 feet, allowing classes to fill up with students like it was 2019. But we are not done just yet. Union contracts still dictate 6 feet between desks and the administration is citing numerous logistical challenges. Many things about the entire reopening process were opaque. Schedules were created with fewer hours of in-person instruction than parents expected due to surprise blockers with little explanation. Hundreds of questions sent to the school board remain unanswered. Memoranda of understanding with unions were arrived at after negotiation and then celebrated and approved at school board meetings. Negotiations between administrators and teachers are a window into both what the administration is looking for and what unions are looking for. Keeping that entire process hidden was a key contributor to the frustration and surprises that many hundreds of parents and students felt. I was curious about why this process was so secretive, unlike much more open negotiations in other unionized industries, like healthcare. It was suggested that I learn about the Rodda Act, known formally as EERA. It is named after its sponsor, former State Senator Albert Rodda. The EERA is regulated by the California Public Employment Relations Board

A little-known provision in the Rodda Act mandates that school districts reveal the initial bargaining positions of both sides at a public school board meeting, allow public input on what the administration should be asking for, and the school board vote on their initial proposal. All of these steps have to occur prior to the start of the negotiation. Unfortunately, Piedmont Unified never followed this procedure. This sunshine clause was enacted as Government Code 3547 and was used correctly by at least one other school district, Fremont Unified. This law is very clear, helpful, and should be followed. articles.text: This past week our country has witnessed a heartbreaking continuation of violence focused on people of Asian descent. Recent attacks against those of Asian descent have been traumatic. The deadly shooting in Atlanta last week understandably increases the concern, fear, and trauma especially for our Asian community. Furthermore, these disturbing attacks are targeting the most vulnerable in our communities. As your Chief of Police, I want our entire community, and particularly our community members of Asian descent, to know their police department stands with them. We have been following these events closely and have been in contact with the Oakland Police Department and our other county partners. I have also made it a priority to reach out to local community stakeholders and representatives of the Piedmont Asian American Club (PAAC) to offer my support following these intolerable crimes. Any race-based attacks and incidents borne of ignorance will be thoroughly investigated and will not be tolerated in Piedmont. We will coordinate any investigations with the Alameda County District Attorney’s newly formed Special Response Team, which has been assembled to assist local law enforcement and our community with the recent violent attacks. The team, made up of Deputy District Attorneys, inspectors and victim/witness advocates, is in place to support our investigative efforts. Finally, I encourage anyone in our community to speak up and speak out. If you’ve been the target of a race-based attack, please call our police department. Violence against anyone in our community affects us all. We at the Piedmont Police Department will continue to do all we can to support and protect everyone. We are mindful of the specific trauma those of Asian descent are experiencing now. We are in this together. Jeremy Bowers is Chief of Police of the City of Piedmont. articles.text: What to expect when getting your home energy score Any residential home or property that is sold or transferred in Piedmont must now provide a Home Energy Score or a Home Energy Audit to both potential buyers and the city’s Planning and Building Department, following the adoption of Ordinance 751 N.S. The passage of the new Home Energy Assessment Ordinance (Ordinance 751 N.S.) was unanimously approved by the City Council on February 1. The ordinance became effective 30 days later. The expectation is that a Home Energy Assessment will assist homeowners in their efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Over 50 percent of emissions in Piedmont come from residences. The ordinance will also ensure that the community meets standards and goals set in the city’s ambitious Climate Action Plan. Now, when listing a property for sale, a report from a Home Energy Audit, or Score, must be provided to potential buyers and the city. A Home Energy Audit is a detailed report of identified treatments for improving a home’s energy use resulting from a whole-house evaluation, including diagnostic testing using specialized equipment.The Score is based on a standard assessment of energy-related assets, to easily compare energy use across the housing market. Sellers of single-family homes in Piedmont are required to obtain and disclose an Audit or Score, which would estimate the energy-related use, associated costs, and cost-effective solutions to improve the home’s efficiency. Getting a Home Energy Score involves a few simple steps that can be accomplished while still living in the home. You can schedule a home energy assessment by contacting an authorized Home Energy Assessor before listing, or otherwise announcing your home for sale. Once you choose an assessment company, a Home Energy Assessor will visit your home to assess it. They will collect information about a home’s foundation, insulation, walls, and windows, as well as its heating, cooling, and water systems. To prepare for your assessment, make sure the assessor has clear access to your garage, basement, and attic, as well as any crawl spaces within the home. The U.S. Department of Energy recommends also providing any records on energy improvement you’ve made to your home already. This includes insulations, the installation of solar paneling, or new furnaces. Once the assessor has completed the evaluation, they will provide you with a Home Energy Score promptly, usually within a few days. The report you receive will provide a list of recommended home energy upgrades. Completing a Home Energy Audit is often a more expensive and lengthy process than the Home Energy Score, according to Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. An audit may take several hours depending on the size of the home, with the auditor employing equipment such as infrared cameras and a blower door test. Coupled with computer modeling, these tools are used to analyze a more detailed assessment of a home’s energy use. For more information, contact the Piedmont Planning Department at 420-3039. pages.text: Wednesday, March 24, 2021 3 Curbing consumption through Piedmont’s Climate Challenge By Nate Redinbo Do you care about climate change? Do you want to make a difference, but you’re not quite sure how? Taking action can be easy, educational, and truly impactful. In Piedmont, over 50% of greenhouse gas emissions come from daily household activities. If you choose to change your habits, you are making a very real impact in the fight to save the planet. Unfortunately, even though the entire global community will be affected by climate change, most of the causes stem from the global wealthy. Wealthy countries such as the U.S. consume far more than poorer countries, and this increased consumption of food, goods, services, and transit have dramatically increased greenhouse gas emissions. Home Energy Assessment Ordinance now in effect What to expect when getting your home energy score By Allyson Aleksey Any residential home or property that is sold or transferred in Piedmont must now provide a Home Energy Score or a Home Energy Audit to both potential buyers and the city’s Planning and Building Department, following the adoption of Ordinance 751 N.S. The passage of the new Home Energy Assessment Ordinance (Ordinance 751 N.S.) was unanimously approved by the City Council on February 1. The ordinance became effective 30 days later. The expectation is that a Home Energy Assessment will assist homeowners in their efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Over 50 percent of emissions in Piedmont come from residences. The ordinance will also ensure that the community meets standards and goals set in the city’s ambitious Climate Action Plan. Now, when listing a property for sale, a report from a Home Energy Audit, or Score, must be provided to potential buyers and the city. A Home Energy Audit is a detailed report of identified treatments for improving a home’s energy use resulting from a whole-house evaluation, including diagnostic testing using specialized equipment.The Score is based on a standard assessment of energy-related assets, to easily compare energy use across the housing market. Sellers of single-family homes in Piedmont are required to obtain and disclose an Audit or Score, which would estimate the energy-related use, associated costs, and cost-effective solutions to improve the home’s efficiency. Getting a Home Energy Score involves a few simple steps that can be accomplished while still living in the home. You can schedule a home energy assessment by contacting an authorized Home Energy Assessor before listing, or otherwise announcing your home for sale. Once you choose an assessment company, a Home Energy Assessor will visit your home to assess it. They will collect information about a home’s foundation, insulation, walls, and windows, as well as its heating, cooling, and water systems. To prepare for your assessment, make sure the assessor has clear access to your garage, basement, and attic, as well as any crawl spaces within the home. The U.S. Department of Energy recommends also providing any records on energy improvement you’ve made to your home already. This includes insulations, the installation of solar paneling, or new furnaces. Once the assessor has completed the evaluation, they will provide you with a Home Energy Score promptly, usually within a few days. The report you receive will provide a list of recommended home energy upgrades. Completing a Home Energy Audit is often a more expensive and lengthy process than the Home Energy Score, according to Piedmont Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman. An audit may take several hours depending on the size of the home, with the auditor employing equipment such as infrared cameras and a blower door test. Coupled with computer modeling, these tools are used to analyze a more detailed assessment of a home’s energy use. For more information, contact the Piedmont Planning Department at 420-3039. articles.text: Editor: The League of Women Voters of California condemns all xenophobic and hateful acts targeting Asian American and Pacific Islander (AAPI) communities. We stand in solidarity with, and in support of AAPI communities in calling for an end to anti-Asian hate and violence. No person, or group of people, should have to live in fear because of who they are. Our hearts are with the loved ones of those lost in Atlanta. We stand with AAPI people everywhere who are experiencing fear, sadness, loss, and anger as they are impacted by not only the domestic terror attack in Atlanta, but the attacks on AAPI communities everywhere. The tragic murders in Atlanta punctuates an increase in antiAsian violence and hate we have seen across the country. Systemic racism and white supremacy in the US are not bound by state or city lines - they are everywhere. California is no exception. Anti-Asian hate crimes within California have been on the rise. It is the responsibility of allies everywhere to vocally denounce hate, violence, and xenophobia and actively work to dismantle the systems of racism and white supremacy that have perpetuated these attitudes and actions in our country. We are committed to listening to and amplifying AAPI voices and educating ourselves on the historic and ongoing systemic racism that plagues this country so that we can be better allies. We urge our followers to do the same, and to call on elected and appointed officials at all levels of government to demonstrate their commitment to keeping ALL communities safe. Please visit StopAAPIHate.org and be part of the solution. There can be no liberty in the face of racist and xenophobic violence. articles.text: Alameda County opens eligibility to people with COVID-19 comorbidities Over half of Piedmont has received at least one dose of COVID-19 vaccine as of March 20, and about one-third of the City’s population is fully vaccinated, according to data from the Alameda County Public Health Department (ACPHD). In recent days, Alameda County has joined other Californian counties in opening vaccine eligibility to people aged 16 to 64 years old “who are deemed to be at the very highest risk due to complex health conditions,” the county’s website states. While the state began permitting healthcare providers to vaccinate individuals with health conditions back on Monday, March 15, the county waited several days to expand eligibility due to supply constraints. The county reports that 4,384 Piedmonters – 52.7 percent of the City’s adult population – have received at least one dose and 2,730 Piedmonters, 32.8 percent of the City, have been fully vaccinated. Vaccines created by Moderna and Pfizer require two doses administered several weeks apart. A recently approved vaccine manufactured by Johnson & Johnson requires only one dose, but just a few thousand doses of this vaccine have arrived in the county so far. Much more are expected to arrive in the coming days. Piedmont leads Alameda County in terms of vaccinated population, but rates across the county have increased in recent weeks. In all of Alameda County, about 683,000 total doses have been administered and around 19 percent of the county’s population is fully vaccinated. In Oakland, about 35 percent of the population has received at least one dose and 18 percent have been fully vaccinated. Over the past seven days, the county began vaccinating residents with health conditions that put them more at risk for COVID-19 mortality. The severe health conditions include cancer, kidney disease, down syndrome, pregnancy, sickle cell disease, heart conditions, severe obesity and several other comorbidities. The full list can be found at the ACPHD website at covid-19. After people with comorbidities, the county is moving to an age-based priority framework in determining vaccine eligibility. Contra Costa and Solano counties already have expanded eligibility to people aged 50 and above. Vaccines should be available to all Californians who want one in the coming months. The state’s guidelines now say “all Californians should have access to COVID-19 vaccines by spring 2021.” President Joe Biden, bolstered by the rising supply rates of the Johnson and Johnson and other vaccines, announced this month that all American adults should be eligible for vaccination by May 1. Pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca announced this week that it has applied to the Food and Drug Administration for emergency use authorization for its COVID-19 vaccine, another vaccine that requires only one dose. Once approved, adding a fourth manufacturer to the effort would greatly increase the nation’s supply. California has administered about 15.2 million vaccine doses out of a stockpile of about 19.3 million doses as of this week, according to the California Department of Public Health. The state is vaccinating an average of over 285,000 people per day. About 20 million Californians are now eligible for the vaccine, a little over half of the state’s population. acgov.org/vaccines.page. Furthermore, people aged 65 years and older have been eligible for weeks. Essential workers in healthcare, food, agriculture, education, childcare, emergency services, public transportation and air travel are eligible. Additionally, those working or living in congregate living facilities, including people experiencing homelessness, are eligible. Residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider, employer or the county to receive a vaccination appointment. California is encouraging residents to utilize the digital “My Turn” notification tool at myturn.ca.gov to determine their vaccine eligibility and schedule appointments.

articles.text: California moved three Bay Area counties – Marin, San Francisco and Santa Clara – into a less restrictive tier for reopening yesterday, Tuesday, March 23, but Alameda County was not among them. These three counties join San Mateo County in the Orange Tier, or Moderate Tier, for reopening their economies due to declining COVID-19 cases. While Alameda County has met the benchmarks for moving to the Orange Tier for over a week, the state waits two weeks for counties to meet thresholds before moving tiers. California moved Alameda County into the Red Tier last Tuesday, March 9 as new cases of COVID-19 decrease in the area. The Red Tier, or Substantial Tier, is the second-most restrictive tier in the state’s four-tier color-coded metric. Before that, the county was in the Purple, or Widespread, Tier – the most restrictive tier. Indoor dining, movie theaters, museums and gyms are allowed for counties in the Red Tier. Small private gathers among no more than three households are permitted indoors, although gathering outdoors is strongly encouraged. In the Orange Tier, the capacity limits for indoor activities increase and non-essential offices can open at 25 percent capacity. In Marin, San Francisco and Santa Clara counties, these changes will go into place today, Wednesday, March 24. The rolling seven-day positive percentage for COVID-19 tests in Alameda County dipped to 1.2 percent as of Monday, March 23 – its lowest point since the pandemic began a year ago. The positivity rate is now below an earlier nadir in October before the worst surge of the pandemic seen so far hit in the winter. The county meets the positivity rate benchmark to move into the Orange Tier – it will need to stay below 4.9 percent for Alameda County to move tiers. The number of cases per 100,000 people needs to be below 3.9 – right now there are 3.3 cases per 100,000. The positivity rate in census-designated low-income areas also needs to be below 5.2 percent – it is currently 2.4 percent in Alameda County. One new case was reported in Piedmont over the past seven days, the second case recorded in the City in March. In total, there have been 170 COVID-19 cases reported in Piedmont. Across Alameda County, the total caseload for the county is 82,747, less than a 1 percent increase week-over-week. There have been 25,706 cases recorded in Oakland and 12,984 cases in Hayward. There have been 1,370 deaths caused by COVID-19 countywide. While many health experts are cautiously optimistic about the current course of the pandemic, there are calls for the public to remain vigilant with mask use and social distancing as new variants of COVID-19 are identified around the state. As of press time, the California Department of Public Health reported that there have been 3,549,101 total cases of COVID- 19 in California. There have been 56,596 deaths due to the disease statewide.

articles.text: A year away from campus has been devastating for many students. Zoom fatigue, lack of social contact, and not enough personal interaction with teachers is driving them crazy. They are desperate to get back to school and to their friends and daily routines as soon as possible. But not all students are eager to go back. The thing that has surprised me most throughout the pandemic is the fact that some of my students are thriving at home. For them, not having to summon the energy for superficial social interactions at school is a huge benefit to remote learning, as is not feeling depleted at the end of a bustling day on campus. Being in the relative quiet of their own homes, and having time to luxuriate in their own thoughts, has been a gift this past year. And some of them don’t want to give it up. Take Alexa, for instance. Alexa transitioned to remote learning effortlessly. She was able to stay motivated with her coursework because she no longer experienced the social anxiety that used to consume her when she was on campus. At home, she doesn’t worry about saying the wrong thing, or not looking perfect--common teenage preoccupations that kept her on edge during in-person learning. Alexa has blossomed in the comfort of her own home, something her teachers and peers have noticed. Not all students want to return to school So how can parents help students like Alexa—the introverts—readjust to a return to campus? First, if your child is an introvert, and if they have liked being at home, start by acknowledging this fact. Especially for older students, those who consume a lot of media and understand the national push to return to campus, they may feel hesitant to share their feelings. Being an introvert is a challenge at school, and so let them know their feelings are normal. Second, honor their introversion. This is especially important if parent(s) are extroverts and aren’t hardwired to love peace, quiet, and solitude. As your child transitions back to school, consider creating introverted family rituals, like reading books in the same room, or having planned quiet time during family activities, such as car rides or walks. Finally, make sure your introverted child has ample time in the evenings and on weekends to recover from the energy-drain that is school. Don’t push them to be social or engage in too many activities. Let them readjust to the “real” world, which is a very extroverted world, at their own pace. They will thank you for it. Dr. Susan Eva Porter is the Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at sue@orindaacademy.org.
articles.title: Some students are thriving learning at home

articles.text: In the dark cloud of a pandemic, it can be tough to find the silver lining. As hard as it’s been, 17-year-old pianist Liam Charron says it’s also been helpful. He’s been able to focus, practice, learn and compose like never before. “Music is a conversation between you and other people, and when there are no other people, you struggle to find meaning in it,” said the Piedmont High School senior. “But without Covid, I think I would not have been the player I am now.” Just prior to California’s shelter-in-place order one year ago, Charron wasn’t all that motivated, he said. But then he toured some colleges where he could pursue his love of music with a major in jazz studies with a focus on piano. “Seeing the end goal with my own eyes made all the difference,” he said. “That’s when I decided: I’m going to hunker down and do this. So I started practicing much longer, much smarter in some ways. I’ve had so much more improvement … than I could have imagined.” A member of the Jazz Band and Jazz Combo at PHS, Charron started with piano more than 10 years ago, and has since learned to play other instruments. He used downtime last summer to accomplish a major goal — an album on Spotify. “I played all the instruments, I sang all the vocals,” he said. “I had to judge my own content, but Piedmont senior and pianist Liam Charron. it was really good, because with every song I grew and got more confident and put new things in.” Now that the college application process is finished, Charron is working on his piano technique, transcribing the music of jazz greats like Bill Evans, and exploring the compositional aspects of playing ballads. “I’ve been learning things that I’ve been wanting to learn,” he said. “There’s no point to stop learning now.” Kristen Hatcher is a member of the Piedmont Arts Fund, which supports visual and performing arts programs for students in Piedmont schools.
articles.title: Pandemic can’t stop this Piedmont musician

articles.text: On March 17, Mills College president Elizabeth Hillman announced that the school will no longer enroll first-year students. Located in Oakland, Mills College is a nationally renowned liberal arts college for women and gender-binary students. The college was founded as the Young Ladies Seminary in 1852 and was the first women’s college west of the Rockies. It currently offers more than 45 undergraduate majors and minors, as well as 30 graduate degrees, certificates, and credentials. Beginning this year, the college will phase out its degree programs to instead become Mills Institute. It will hand out its last degrees in 2023. Hillman explained that “the economic burdens of the COVID- 19 pandemic, structural changes across higher education, and budget deficits” led to the decision. Mills has weathered years of financial instability and declining enrollment. Currently, the prestigious college enrolls just about 900 students, a roughly 30 percent decline since 2015. The college is beginning to transition its academic programs by creating options and degree pathways for all Mills students, Hillman explained. The Provost’s Office will develop plans for each degree program that the college currently offers. The Admissions Office will serve a role in supporting students who pursue transfer opportunities outside Mills College. “While Mills’ role as a degree-granting college will end, its mission will endure. Mills intends to continue to foster women’s leadership and student success, advance gender and racial equity, and cultivate innovative pedagogy, research, and critical thinking by creating a Mills Institute housed here on campus,” Hillman said. “This year, faculty, trustees, staff, students, and other community stakeholders will consider potential structures and programming for the proposed institute,” she added. U.S Rep. Barbara Lee (Oakland), a Mills graduate, said in a statement that she was “heartbroken and outraged” by the announcement. “Personally, I owe a debt of gratitude to Mills College. Five decades ago, I was able to attend college and earn a degree as a young single mother on public assistance, who often had to bring her sons to class - something that would have been impossible at many other colleges and universities,” Lee said. She added that Mills College was where she met her mentor, Congresswoman Shirley Chisholm, and where her “passion for public service and politics began.” The school has been essential in recruiting underrepresented students, Lee said. In 2014, Mills College became the first single-sex college in the United States to adopt an admission policy explicitly welcoming transgender students. Fifty-six percent of current undergraduate students self-identify as students of color.
articles.title: Mills College to discontinue granting degrees

articles.text: Governor Gavin Newsom visited Ruby Bridges Elementary School in Alameda on Tuesday, March 16, to discuss the state’s progress toward reopening campuses. Ruby Bridges Elementary and other schools in the city of Alameda welcomed students back for in-person instruction on March 15. During his visit, Gov. Newsom said that about 9,000 of California’s nearly 11,000 public schools have reopened or announced dates to reopen this spring. But, like Piedmont, Alameda Unified’s reopening is only a partial “hybrid” model. On March 1, Gov. Newsom and lawmakers forged a $6.6 billion reopening bill. He stated that, after the height of the winter surge in COVID-19 cases, the conversation shifted from “whether to reopen schools, to when.” Since the governor’s announcement, the state has collaborated with county health departments, the Biden Administration and providers such as Kaiser Permanente to accelerate vaccine access for K-12 school staff. Access to vaccination proved to be a significant hurdle in reopening some districts, particularly Los Angeles Unified. The bill allocates $2 billion to fund safety measures that support in-person instruction, such as personal protective equipment, ventilation upgrades and COVID-19 testing. A proposed $4.6 billion will fund expanded learning opportunities, such as summer school, tutoring, and mental health services. The bill also requires that, by April 1, all California public schools offer “in-person instruction to grades K-2 for all students, [or] lose one percent of eligible funds every day thereafter if they do not.” Districts that don’t open by May 15 will lose eligibility for funding. This money should provide incentives for reopening; however, no language in the bill mandates reopening. “We are seeing real progress, real momentum,” Newsom told Photo by Jeff Chiu, Associated Press reporters at Ruby Bridges Elementary School. He attributed reopening success to “plummeting COVID-19 case rates statewide.” About 80 percent of students voluntarily returned to Ruby Bridges Elementary on March 15, a number that Newsom said he expects will grow. “Parents need to have confidence [to send kids back], not just the teachers, the custodial staff, bus drivers, or the folks that make schools like this work,” he said. According to California’s Safe Schools for All Plan, Piedmont Unified has received $1,057,073 in state funding, and three months worth of PPE. The district provided a safety plan to the California Department of Health on January 31, 2021.

The Provost’s Office will develop plans for each degree program that the college currently offers. The Admissions Office will serve a role in supporting students who pursue transfer opportunities outside Mills College. “While Mills’ role as a degree-granting college will end, its mission will endure. Mills intends to continue to foster women’s leadership and student success, advance gender and racial equity, and cultivate innovative pedagogy, research, and critical thinking by creating a Mills Institute housed here on campus,” Hillman said. “This year, faculty, trustees, staff, students, and other community stakeholders will consider potential structures and programming for the proposed institute,” she added. articles.text: It’s been 53 weeks since I last set foot on campus. Not in the shortcut-to-Mulberry’s way; I’ve done plenty of that, when my mom couldn’t handle the lockdown cooking anymore and sent me to buy lunch, but in the real, go-to-school way. Walking to school on March 19, 2021, one year and one week after Piedmont schools had closed due to Covid-19 pandemic, I was nervous that I was forgetting something, especially forgetting something of importance. I was correct: I forgot my computer and felt like an idiot. But can you blame me? I hadn’t been on campus for over a year! As I walked onto campus and saw real people again, it was as if I was a little kid and just got a puppy for my birthday. People I hadn’t seen in the flesh for so long had been only small moving figures on my computer. To be sure, like the rest of Piedmont I was shocked to learn that in the reopening plan my middle school day would be a measly two hours, and only once a week. But I guess even that was better than nothing. Why Piedmont Middle School has been singled out to have the shortest school week on the planet is anyone’s guess. On the first day of going back to in-person learning, I was all over the place. In the morning I had an online class and after that I would be going to school. My sister, who tore herself away from checking college acceptances on various portals, helped me pick out an outfit, so that I could look like a model. During quarantine, I had been trying on various entertainments for my lonely self, and modeling is the latest. I figured that I’d walk those school halls like I was at London Fashion Week. (As model Kendall Jenner said, “The world is your runway.”) On my way to school, I met up with my friend, and we walked together. As we reached Wildwood playground for our shortcut to the middle school, we discovered that that the gate had been locked. We were already late, so if we took an alternate route we would have arrived even later. So, I may or may not have climbed a fence to open the gate from inside. Next up was racing up the PE Hill with two masks: no easy feat. Once on campus, I was awestruck: people milled around getting to and from class, friends chatted to each other, teachers talked about their classes – like a dream from times in the past. As I walked up the stairs to my math classroom, I couldn’t stop thinking: “This is really happening; I am back in school.” During my first real class of the year, while our math teacher talked about triangles, I found myself watching the kids in the room. Seated in the back, I could easily see everyone. I saw friends talking to each other while doing their class project, as well as those just doing their work and occasionally asking a person next to them for help. It was strangely comforting to see everyone interacting with each other after a year apart. My math teacher also looked quite happy: he could finally see his students again. As I walked to my second class of the day, I soaked in the environment that I had been deprived of for too long. It was funny to see classmates yelling so they could be heard. After all, we have learned that it’s extremely hard to hear someone talking through two masks. As I searched for the classroom, I was surprised I didn’t find Narnia after walking into the janitors’ closets on accident. Hard to believe, but I had forgotten my way around my own school. When I finally got there, it was the same as the math class. Kids were enjoying being around one another. Although I couldn’t exactly see their faces because of the masks, I could tell that everyone was happy. After the class was over while walking to meet my friend, I felt like I really just had a completely normal day. It felt like there was no COVID – it was just a bunch of teenagers going to school. As far as safety goes, the middle school did an amazing job. There was proper spacing between all the desks, hand sanitizers everywhere, and arrows on the floor to direct you safely to your next class. The flaw with the arrows part was it was all one way, so if you walked past your class you had to walk around the entire school again. Jimmy took a wrong turn, and some say that he is still trying to find his science class. Otherwise, it has been as planned to the last detail. If you needed hand sanitizer, a bottle of it would be within five feet, no matter where you were. A new mask? No problem; go ask a teacher. Overall I am extremely excited to go be back in school and to actually learn something. Thank you to everyone who made it possible to be able to get back on campus. Thank you to the teachers who have been doing their best to make distance learning bearable. I can’t wait to go back to full-time classes in the fall. articles.text: After months of sheltering at home due to the Covid pandemic, Piedmont Scouts in Troop 15 are getting together to explore the great outdoors. Last Sunday morning, March 21, a big group of 55 members of Scouts and Scout leaders rode their bicycles along the Bay Trail from Oyster Bay Regional Shoreline (near the west end of Davis Street in San Leandro) to the San Mateo Bridge, a 12-mile round trip. articles.text: Andy Melian records 2 sacks, 7 tackles for loss The Friday night lights were on at Witter Field in a big welcome back to varsity football for Piedmont High. In their season home opener on March 19, the Highlanders went to double overtime against Castro Valley before winning 20-14. Senior running back Brian Cain punched in the game-winner from the one-yard line. “We’ve been practicing all winter and the kids were excited just to have a game. Just to win was huge for us and builds our confidence. Hopefully we can build more confidence against Mt. Eden [next week], but not make it so hard,” said PHS coach Jerome Johnson with a nervous chuckle. Senior defensive lineman Andy Melian wreaked havoc against the Trojans, with two sacks, seven tackles for loss, and 11 total tackles. He also blocked a Castro Valley extra point attempt. “It was a fun game. Our defensive line has been together nearly Senior lineman Mason Kimball (78) had 1.5 sacks, a leaping pass deflection, and a punt return. all four years and I think we’re bringing things together this year. It feels like we’re really meshing,” said Melian. Alongside him on the defensive line is junior Mason Kimball, providing a second clear anchor for Piedmont. Kimball recorded 1.5 sacks, a critical leaping pass defense in the third quarter, and even caught a botched punt for a slight return in the second quarter “It felt great to be back out there after not playing football for a year and a half. I never thought I’d catch a punt return. It’s probably the most I’ve touched the ball in a game,” said Kimball. Although the game finished in heated fashion, PHS had the game in control at halftime with a 14-0 lead. Cain, the senior captain, made the Highlanders’ first two scores, one on offense and other while playing defense. He scored a TD from the three-yard line with 6:56 left in the first quarter. He also had the play of the game on defense before halftime. articles.text: Ellie Black wins 1600 & 3200; Jack Stein wins 3200 The Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Berkeley High on Wednesday, March 17 for a dual meet with the Yelllowjackets. The Highlanders won 11 events, including Ellie Black winning the 1600 and 3200, and Jack Stein and Seamus Chamberlain-Carr placed 1st and 2nd with times of 10:23 and 10:24, one second apart. The two runners have led their teams since the start of the season. Black, who was the Post’s Sophomore of the Year in 2020, clocked a personal record time in the 1600 meters in 5:47.1, a 7-second improvement from her time one year ago. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team improved its record to 2-1 after winning two consecutive games with great pitching coupled with late-hitting heroics. PHS recorded a 2-0 win against the visiting Oakland Tech Bulldogs on a sunny Saturday, March 20, and followed that with a 5-4 victory over Mt. Eden two days later. On Saturday, pitcher Cal Barna threw 12 strikeouts in six innings, while reliever Julian Scherman gained a save to close out the win in the seventh. Monday featured Ben Levinson throwing five innings with 11 strikeouts and just one hit; Scherman gained the victory. But as good as coach Eric Olson’s pitching staff is proving, the Highlanders’ bats have come through when it mattered most. Piedmont’s 2-0 victory against Tech featured sophomore Michael Aikawa hitting a game-winning RBI double in the bottom of the fifth. In the victory over Mt. Eden, senior slugger Lars Derr hit the game-winning RBI to the right field fence at Witter Field in the bottom of the seventh. 2-0 win over Oakland Tech Barna was dealing heat on the mound in Saturday’s victory against the Bulldogs. The University of Hawaii-bound player showed confidence on the mound, effectively mixing his arsenal of pitches between fastball, slider, sinker, changeup, and curveball. He made sure to praise catcher Davis Alazraqui for his performance as well. “I woke up feeling good and ready to play. My catcher [Davis Alazraqui] played great. Getting out of those first-inning jitters and Davis doing so well behind the plate made it even better. In the third, fourth, and fifth,” said Barna. The game remained scoreless through five innings, but a oneout double by Michael Aikawa broke the scoring drought in the bottom of the fifth. articles.text: Filoli House and Garden in Woodside. Filoli House and Gardens is hosting a virtual, botanical art graduate exhibit. Each artist chose a theme represented in five separate paintings. Themes range from the native buckeye, to the joy of cooking with vegetables. A total of ten botanical artists participated, all graduates of Filoli’s botanical art certificate program. The program includes over 200 hours of class and homework, then an average of 12 months on their final project. articles.text: Cristiana Pegoraro, a world-renowned pianist from Narnia, Italy, who has performed in Piedmont, has received United Nations patronage for her new music video release of “Rain.” Composed and performed by Pegoraro, “Rain” commemorates World Water Day, which has been celebrated on March 22 by the United Nations every year since 1992. Through her music, the pianist brings attention to our consumption of the valuable resource. The video features beautiful landscapes of Pegoraro’s homeland Umbria, a lush Italian region bordering Tuscany. The magnificent Marmore Waterfall and Lake Piediluco are the backdrop for “Rain.” The video was produced by Imprenditori di Sogni and directed by Yuri Napoli and Adriano Natale. This year’s theme is about what water means to people, its true value, and how we can better protect the resource. Pegoraro’s work Christiana Pegoraro in “Rain” is a tribute to Umbria, as well as a gift to “those who make themselves active and caring guardians.” “This work was a new experience, a way to express myself during the pandemic,” Pegoraro said. “When I was unable to perform and travel the world for concerts and activities, I brought my creativity to a new path and enriched my artistic vein of new stimuli.” To watch “Rain,” visit https:// www.youtube.com/watch?v=euPtUtEMqlo.
articles.title: Christiana Pegoraro’s music receives U.N. Patronage for World Water Day

articles.text: Berkeley Symphony has announced the launch of REAL Berkeley, a four-episode virtual film series that feature special guests from the Berkeley community, through curators, local videography, and chamber music performed by musicians of the orchestra. The series will begin Sunday, March 28 at 4 p.m. with writer and curator Kate Schatz. Schatz, a feminist writer, activist and educator, is the creator of the Rad Women book series, along with illustrator Miriam Klein Stahl. Her children’s book, Rad American Women A-Z, was published by the well known Bay Area-publisher City Lights in Spring 2015, and was on the New York Times bestseller list for 11 weeks. The first episode will feature three works by prominent female composers: Reena Esmail’s Meri Sakhi Ki Avaaz (My Sister’s Voice), Gabriella Smith’s Tessellations and Clara Shumann’s Piano Trio. The next episode will be released on May 16. REAL Berkeley is produced by Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director Rene Mandel, in partnership with Symphony Music Director Joseph Young and Bay Area-based media company Reneff-Olson Productions. The series will shine a light on unique aspects of Berkeley that have had a positive and significant impact on both the orchestra, and its community members. “The importance of a strong and resilient community has been displayed throughout the past year as residents, businesses, organizations, and many others have all come together to provide support for one another during these difficult times,” Mandel said. “REAL Berkeley pays tribComposer Reena Esmail ute to a community that we are proud to represent. We look forward to celebrating these wonderful aspects of our city through adventurous music and imagery that represent the diversity and ethos of Berkeley.” Visit https://www.berkeleysymphony.org/ for more information on how to watch the upcoming series.

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Perhaps every generation lives through some form of revolution that alters, sometimes profoundly, how they live. Imagine the seismic shifts caused by the Gutenberg press, electricity, the telephone, flight, or the car. We are living through a communication-techno revolution that continues to impact countless facets of our lives. The computer, in all its permutations, has changed everything, and there is no going back. The worldwide web, the online world, the hardware and the software, represent a gestalt that is reconfiguring our society and the world community in ways that we are still trying to comprehend. Just seven years ago the concept of a social network called Facebook was unimaginable. A sophomore sitting in a Harvard dorm room with some friends did imagine it. And in 2010 a movie arrived about those nascent years. We are told, some 500 million people have joined this electronic community of suggested intimacy. The Social Network is a remarkable film, written by Aaron Sorkin, creator of West Wing, a superb wordsmith whose signature style includes intelligent, snappy dialogue. The narrative is driven by conversation, in dorm rooms, sitting in front of screens, and in conference rooms where depositions are being taken, conversations that reveal the complexity and animosities and intentions of the many compelling characters. It’s simply wonderful writing, for which Sorkin received an Academy Award in 2010 for Best Screenplay. One example takes place in the opening scene between the film’s protagonist, Mark Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg), and his girlfriend, Erica (Rooney Mara), over beers in a Harvard hangout. The brief encounter is revelatory, and frames nicely Zuckerberg’s arrogant, enigmatic, computer persona. It’s a wonderful beginning to what proves to be an engaging story. At first blush, a narrative about the founding of Facebook would seem to lack intensity, peopled by nerds who can write computer code and understand algorithm apps. And yet because Andrew Garfield as Eduardo Saverin and Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in David Fincher’s The Social Network. of David Fincher’s top drawer directing (Fight Club, Seven, Zodiac) and Sorkin’s dynamite script – based on the book, Accidental Billionaires by Ben Mezrich – the movie transcends the esoteric and captures the unsettling mood of a generation. The movie is filled with irony and is a study in contrasts. While Zuckerberg is brilliant seated in front of his computer, and shows flashes of real genius, he can’t marshal the skills to even adequately engage with others. Yet counterintuitively he constructs a network that is predicated on the desire to interact with others. His story turns out to be a riveting though often unflattering character study in which his one friend, the co-founder of Facebook, Eduardo Saverin (Andrew Garfield), is forced to sue Zuckerberg for his rightful share of the company. It’s tempting to extrapolate from the phenomenon known as Facebook (now a verb), and wonder if for all of our unrelenting contact with one another – cell phones, twitter, texting, social networking – are we not still caught in a riptide of loneliness and angst for which ultimately there is no antidote? If you have not seen the trailer to The Social Network, google “Choral version of Radio Head’s Creep.” Click on the first listing and you will view not only a preview of the film, but hear the haunting choral soundtrack performed by Scala, a Belgian choir, led by the Kolachny brothers, one directing the other on piano. It captures perfectly the tone of the film. A variation of this trailer should have been used before the final credits rolled, it’s that good. The Social Network (2010). Directed by David Fincher, with screenplay by Alan Sorkin. Starring Jason Eisenberg, Andrew Garfield, Justin Timberlake and Arnie Hammer. 2 hrs., 1 min. Rated PG-13

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré The White Ribbon, nominated in 2009 for an Oscar for Best Foreign Language Film (from Germany), won the Palm d’Or at Cannes for Best Feature Film. Directed by Michael Haneke (Cache), it is artful, superbly cast, and beautifully photographed in stark black and white. The year is 1913, on the cusp of World War I. The film opens with a lovely shot of farmers and villagers harvesting the summer wheat, followed by a celebration heralding the end of one season and the beginning of another. It’s tempting to romanticize this bucolic setting – a small town surrounded by the flat expanse of rural northern Germany, filled with hardworking people whose lives follow the rhythms of the land. But then Haneke grimly pulls back a curtain and reveals that behind this seemingly benign image is a bleak and cruel reality that is astonishing in its severity. There is no overt violence in the film except for a set piece in the first minutes of act one when a doctor, riding home on his horse, is brought down by an all but invisible trip wire. At first the incident, called an accident, seems an aberration. But then other events take place of equal premeditation, testimony to the fact that a malevolent and mysterious perpetrator resides in the village. Though these chilling acts of violence are linchpins throughout the film, what is far more disturbing is the authoritarian, patriarchal cruelty leveled against the village’s children. The adults, charged with loving them, are so consistently perverse in their anger and punishments that it’s as if we’re watching and exorcism of their childhood innocence. In a particularly unsettling scene, the village Pastor, blinded by his own narrow Protestantism, ties white ribbons around the arms of his children as reminders that they have violated his trust, betrayed their purity, and disappointed their parents. He will not remove the ribbons until they have demonstrated that they are pure once again. The ribbons torment the children and are reminders of the hypocrisy and heartlessness of those adults to whom the children look for protection and, yes, love. The f ilm also answers Haneke’s own question: is the heart of man inherently dark? His answer is, in frame after frame, an unequivocal yes. He also asks the audience to extrapolate from the microcosm of this small village to the fascism that eventually grips all of Germany. To contemplate The White Ribbon is to feel simultaneously revulsion and admiration. Overly long (almost 2 ½ hours), unrelentingly dour and forbidding, it is also unfailingly honest regarding the ability of one generation to do great harm to the next, for reasons that are not limited to one people but to mankind. For some, this film will be more than they want to endure. Others will watch in fascination while being repelled. Regardless, all must acknowledge that Haneke is a superb filmmaker. The White Ribbon. Starring Christian Friedel, Leonie Benesch, Urich Tukur and Ursina Lardi. Directed by Michael Haneke. 2 hrs., 25 min. Rated R

Rated R The Social Network – the revolution of social media Movie review by Chris Honoré Perhaps every generation lives through some form of revolution that alters, sometimes profoundly, how they live. Imagine the seismic shifts caused by the Gutenberg press, electricity, the telephone, flight, or the car. We are living through a communication-techno revolution that continues to impact countless facets of our lives. The computer, in all its permutations, has changed everything, and there is no going back. The worldwide web, the online world, the hardware and the software, represent a gestalt that is reconfiguring our society and the world community in ways that we are still trying to comprehend. Just seven years ago the concept of a social network called Facebook was unimaginable. A sophomore sitting in a Harvard dorm room with some friends did imagine it. And in 2010 a movie arrived about those nascent years. We are told, some 500 million people have joined this electronic community of suggested intimacy. The Social Network is a remarkable film, written by Aaron Sorkin, creator of West Wing, a superb wordsmith whose signature style includes intelligent, snappy dialogue. The narrative is driven by conversation, in dorm rooms, sitting in front of screens, and in conference rooms where depositions are being taken, conversations that reveal the complexity and animosities and intentions of the many compelling characters. It’s simply wonderful writing, for which Sorkin received an Academy Award in 2010 for Best Screenplay. One example takes place in the opening scene between the film’s protagonist, Mark Zuckerberg (Jesse Eisenberg), and his girlfriend, Erica (Rooney Mara), over beers in a Harvard hangout. The brief encounter is revelatory, and frames nicely Zuckerberg’s arrogant, enigmatic, computer persona. It’s a wonderful beginning to what proves to be an engaging story. At first blush, a narrative about the founding of Facebook would seem to lack intensity, peopled by nerds who can write computer code and understand algorithm apps. And yet because Andrew Garfield as Eduardo Saverin and Jesse Eisenberg as Mark Zuckerberg in David Fincher’s The Social Network. of David Fincher’s top drawer directing (Fight Club, Seven, Zodiac) and Sorkin’s dynamite script – based on the book, Accidental Billionaires by Ben Mezrich – the movie transcends the esoteric and captures the unsettling mood of a generation. The movie is filled with irony and is a study in contrasts. While Zuckerberg is brilliant seated in front of his computer, and shows flashes of real genius, he can’t marshal the skills to even adequately engage with others. Yet counterintuitively he constructs a network that is predicated on the desire to interact with others. His story turns out to be a riveting though often unflattering character study in which his one friend, the co-founder of Facebook, Eduardo Saverin (Andrew Garfield), is forced to sue Zuckerberg for his rightful share of the company. It’s tempting to extrapolate from the phenomenon known as Facebook (now a verb), and wonder if for all of our unrelenting contact with one another – cell phones, twitter, texting, social networking – are we not still caught in a riptide of loneliness and angst for which ultimately there is no antidote? If you have not seen the trailer to The Social Network, google “Choral version of Radio Head’s Creep.” Click on the first listing and you will view not only a preview of the film, but hear the haunting choral soundtrack performed by Scala, a Belgian choir, led by the Kolachny brothers, one directing the other on piano. It captures perfectly the tone of the film. A variation of this trailer should have been used before the final credits rolled, it’s that good. The Social Network (2010). Movie review by Chris Honoré Saban’s Power Rangers is an unabashed movie for older teens with lots of CGI action and other wild, over-the-top stuff that kids will love. Personally, I’m a sucker for origin films and the first act (plus part of act two) is a good one. You have five kids who all look like they are on the Student Council but somehow end up in detention, ala The Breakfast Club. Each one feels powerless and definitely misunderstood. And there lies the real story of The Power Rangers and all other comic book movies that take wimpy kids and give them super powers. What adolescent doesn’t wish he or she had some serious mojo? You can start with Spiderman and go through the deep Marvel and DC comics bench and it’s all about power and how it’s used. Kids love this idea. It’s brilliant. In Power Rangers you have five young people who are given the gift (similar to Harry Potter). Now it’s up to them to make use of it. Acts two and three of this nostalgic reboot – based on a 1993 TV series – go nuts with Naomi Watts showing up as ultra-campy Rita Repulsa (how’s that for a name?). She is evil incarnate and wants to lay waste to all, including the bucolic town’s Krispy Kreme donut shop. Really. But here’s the deal: Rangers is all about friendship, bonding, and finally morphing. It’s also got a quirky robot named Alpha 5, portrayed by Bill Harder, as well as a very cool spaceship buried deep in a quarry. I mean, the kids could have gone back to school and hassled some bullies (one does get his mild comeuppance); but they have bigger things to do. Like save their families and their town. This is a popcorn movie. But a good one. And for kids, it’s been a dry spell. They were overdue for a kids’ movie that just goes for it with enthusiasm and has a good heart at its center. articles.text: Film review by Chris Honoré If there was life left in this long-running franchise, which came perilously close to jumping the shark, it had to reside with X-Men, the early years, long before the mutant heroes were galvanized into a world-saving, shape-shifting crew. First Class, released in 2011, is based on the iconic Marvel comic books created by Stan Lee and Jack Kirby. It proves to be good entertainment. It’s always interesting to ask why mutants, aka Superheroes, have such generational appeal, seeming to resonate decade after decade, going back to the 30s. It was 1963 when Lee and Kirby revealed a series of contemporary mutants: Spider-Man, the Hulk, Iron Man, the Fantastic Four, and, of course, the X-Men, all following their antecedents: DC’s Superman (why is it hard to think of Superman as a mutant?) and Batman (a man with lots of suspend-your-disbelief gadgets and a great costume), to name just two. Actually, the list of those with extraordinary powers is huge, creating a comic book genre that has had countless incarnations. X-Men: First Class includes all the usual suspects – only younger. Think of this as “X-Men: Roots.” And, of course, there is the resident villain, pre-Magneto, played nicely by Kevin Bacon. The film opens in a Nazi concentration camp, the year is 1944, and stretches to the Cuban Missile Crisis when the U.S. and Russia played a serious game of chicken. The “X-Men” fans (and their numbers are considerable) should find this film solidly entertaining, a yearbook of their heroes. It has a globe-trotting plot, beginning in Germany and then Russia, Miami, Argentina, London and Las Vegas. Of course, these films increasingly take advantage of stateof-the art special effects. Filmmakers doing comic books and graphic novels must worship at the shrine of CGI. Or at least genuflect. There is nothing that the writers from DC and Marvel can put on paper that the special effects folks can’t put on the screen with stunning realism. They help create stories that teens and pre-teens will enjoy with jaw-dropping enthrallment. Tangentially, it’s hard not to think of these films as being a bit camp, bordering on kitsch. Mutants? Really? But then there is likely not an adolescent out there who can’t identify with these characters in some way. It’s not easy growing up, convinced you’re different. There likely are times when mutant superpowers would come in handy, say, walking down the middle school hall while mind reading. In fact, is it a stretch to think of Harry Potter, magician extraordinaire, and all the residents of Hogwarts, as mutants? An aside: X-Men: First Class is in 2-D. The debate still continues as to whether 3-D really enhances the movie-going experience. It likely pumps up the volume and the revenue, but does it have legs? This “X-Men” is engaging without the glasses and those hyped-up, leap-off-the-screen moments that have become de rigueur. X-Men: First Class. Starring James McAvoy, Michael Fassbinder, January Jones, Rose Byrne, Kevin Bacon and Jennifer Lawrence. Directed by Matthew Vaughn. 2 hrs., 12 min. Rated PG. The highly anticipated annual White Elephant Sale, Oakland Museum of California’s largest fundraiser, will be entirely virtual this year. “We realized that we would not be able to have our traditional White Elephant Sale in the warehouse, with thousands of shoppers and all our volunteers. So we started planning and looking at alternative ways to raise money for the museum,” said Sherry Westernoff, President of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board, a group of over 100 members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has generated over $23 million for the Museum. The White Elephant Sale, touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale, garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont – some of whom are members of the Board. The board has been very fortunate in that they have been able to recruit volunteers with experience in e-commerce and online sales, explained Westernoff. An online store had to be built “from the ground up” in the transition. “We’ve been very lucky in that we have an incredible team of volunteers who are able to get [the virtual sale] up and running,” she said. “A number of our volunteers have been very excited to learn about this new way to sell our items.” The sale traditionally has a one-day Preview Sale a month in advance and two days of the actual Sale. Both events attract thousands of shoppers from the Bay Area and beyond to the white Elephant Sale Warehouse near the Estuary in Oakland’s Fruitvale District. Last year, hundreds of thousands of items were sold, but this year’s virtual sale will be scaled back a bit. “This year will be a smaller version of the traditional sale. We have hand-picked items to post onto our store [website]. We’ll have wonderful items – many very unique treasures and collectables,” Westernoff said. The team of volunteers is also smaller as many volunteers were not able to come into the warehouse due to Alameda County’s stay-at-home order. “The average age of our volunteers is over 65. One of our first priorities was to make sure that our warehouse was set up for social distancing, and that all proper equipment was in place so that our volunteers could come back to a very safe and healthy environment when they were allowed to return,” Westernoff explained. Due to the shutdown in March 2020, volunteers did not return to the warehouse until October, which is typically when volunteers begin planning for the next sale. “There’s usually a one-month break from the previous sale, and then we start all over again. It’s really a year-long operation – a real labor of love,” she said. It’s no secret that COVID-19 and subsequent closures have negatively impacted arts industries, and Oakland Museum is not immune to the fallout. This means that funds raised from this year’s White Elephant Sale are all the more crucial. The 61st sale, held on March 7 and 8 last year, raised over $2.4 million on behalf of OMCA - just one week before the county enacted its shelter-inplace order. That was able to help the museum keep afloat during the closures. “The money we earn from the online store will then go to the museum towards its coming year’s activities and exhibitions. With funding down and the museum still being closed, I think anything that we can raise will be so much appreciated by the Oakland Museum,” Westernoff said. Virtual shoppers can expect many unique treasures that you can only find at a sale like this - everything from antique items, vintage furniture, costume, jewelry, art, and more. The 2021 sale will open online Saturday, May 1, at 8 a.m. and will close on Sunday, May 23 at 6 p.m. There will be over 10,000 items for sale, all available on a first-come basis. Donations for the sale are still being accepted. For a list of items that can be accepted, visit: https:// www.whiteelephantsale.org/ donate. To schedule a pickup for your donation, call 510-839-5919. OMCA is dedicated to the art, history, and natural science of California and contains more than 1.8 million items dedicated to “telling the history of California” within its 110,000 square feet of gallery space. The Museum celebrated its 50th anniversary last year as a leading cultural institution of the Bay Area. The White Elephant Sale is touted as Northern California’s largest rummage sale.

articles.text: Let me take you back in time. It is mid-March 1921. Boxing was yet to have its first million-dollar gate and Babe Ruth was just beginning to make baseball the great American pastime. Football and basketball were minor sports. The great sports personalities of the time were paid peanuts. Ty Cobb, the most famous and feared baseball player of his time, could barely make ends meet with his salary. There was little difference between classical music and pop music. Jazz was just in its early stages of development. So… what was the most popular form of entertainment? It was opera. And opera reigned supreme across every aspect of the population. There were lots of popular opera stars. They were paid thousands of dollars per performance. But nobody was as famous as Enrico Caruso. The paparazzi pestered Caruso just like they do with the stars of today. Caruso often wished he could go out without the long line of paparazzi following him. He would go to a small restaurant in Little Italy with his wife just for a quiet plate of spaghetti and a quiet game of cards with the chef. That made him very happy. There were great singers from the dawn of music. History books give us an idea of what they were able to do. Much of it is astonishing. But we really didn’t know what they sounded like until Edison invented the phonograph. The first singers to record for Edison were born in the 1820s. If you use your imagination, you have a vague idea how they sounded. And then along came Caruso. He single-handedly popularized the recording industry. Everybody started buying records - especially recordings by Caruso. He made so much money that he lived a luxurious life in New York City, where he a had a large suite atop the Knickerbocker Hotel. His summer retreat was the stupendous Bellosguardo estate in Florence, Italy. The public wanted to know everything about their favorite opera star. They knew that he was very generous. He was also one of the greatest caricaturists ever. And in addition to his singing talents, he was a composer and a poet. For all his fame, ironically he had stage fright that was almost paralyzing. Caruso’s career ended exactly 100 years ago, in mid-March 1921. Despite his disciplined work ethic, he simply didn’t take care of himself physically. He ate to excess, and despite good medical advice, he was a chain smoker of expensive Egyptian cigarettes. Those things did him in. He developed pleurisy and had Tenor Enrico Caruso surgery on his lungs. The surgeons operated on him in his suite at the Knickerbocker. The newspapers reported that he was making a good recovery. He returned to his hometown of Naples to recover. But it was too late, and he died five months later in August. My father attended a Caruso performance at the Metropolitan Opera around 1918. His description of the event was one of my greatest inspirations. The recordings give us a faint idea of how glorious his voice was. There are many stories describing what an inspiration he was, always willing to help young singers. One story is particularly funny. During a performance of La Bohème, the soprano singing the part of Mimi was having trouble with her costume. While she was singing, she went behind a large sofa and was able to pull off her slip and then returned to center stage. Caruso, seeing what happened got a mischievous look in his eye. He immediately went behind the sofa and held up the slip for the entire audience to see. The audience burst into laughter. The general director of the Metropolitan Opera disciplined both Caruso and the soprano. She said to Caruso, “Didn’t you know that we would be disciplined?” He replied: “Oh, yes, I knew. But didn’t we have fun!” Listen to some of the old 78 rpm recordings of Enrico Caruso. I think you’ll agree with me that his was a voice for all time. Try to imagine what the voice was like in person, not the fuzzy and scratchy sound that emanates from the primitive recording techniques. Not only did he have a great voice, and a great technique but he made the music come alive. You don’t even need to understand the words. The emotion is evident. As one of the great musicians of the time wrote, “It was one of those portraits that hang in the gallery of memory untarnished by the passing of time.” And now, exactly 100 years later, we can listen to the recordings of Enrico Caruso. His was a life cut short at the age of 47 and yet he lives in that gallery of memories to this very day.

articles.text: Dear Jim: We are considering doing a basement renovation but also would like to do some remodeling on the existing upstairs of our home at the same time. What is the process like for this type of project and what are first steps? How long does it take? Do we need to move out? Thanks for your help with this. –Charles S. Charles: I’ve written recent articles on the topic of basement renovations, but I wanted to take that one step further. What if you also want to work on the rest of your house at the same time? We will look at a recent job we are close to wrapping up to discuss how this went and what you might expect on a typical project. The nature of this job was to do a complete basement dig out and renovation along with a partial remodel of the upstairs including a new master bedroom and bath, new windows, and other cosmetic upgrades. What we encountered here may help you think about questions you may have if you wish to embark on similar projects in the future. Phase 1: The Dig Out For this recent multiple floor remodel, the general workflow involved starting at the bottom and working upwards. While noisy, the basement project alone did not require the clients to move out and they continued to live in the house while working remotely at home. What we call the “dig out” phase involved excavating the basement and crawlspace in its entirety to 9’ to achieve a final height of 8’, along with installing new foundations. It also involved adding exterior drainage, a new The dig out. concrete floor, and the installation of the interior structural walls required to remove the beams and other supports for the upstairs, which were temporary during construction. This part of the work took around 4 months to complete. Phase 2: The more challenging remodel Once the dig out was done, I swapped out our structural crew and brought in the remodeling team. Following the Dig Out, initial work downstairs also involved installing windows, stuccoing the outside, and installing the rest of the interior walls. Then, we completed all of the rough electrical, mechanical and plumbing work. Accommodations were made for tying in the utilities upstairs once we moved out of the basement. Our strategy changed at this point regarding the rest of the work. Because of the house lifting, there were some cracks in the plaster above. We were adding new electrical and mechanical (heating and air conditioning), and our clients wanted special heating registers that required cutting bigger holes in the walls. Given that there were also various plaster textures in different rooms that were going to be hard to duplicate, we decided it would make more sense to tear out the remaining plaster upstairs (except in the kitchen and bath which had already been remodeled). Now that the upstairs work had become more invasive, involving most of the spaces, the client agreed that they would move out for 4 months to allow us to work more effectively there. This new plan allowed us to do a number of things that would have been impossible otherwise, such as insulate the outside walls and the ceilings, add curved archways between some of the common rooms and change some of the trim details. Final Phase: The work nears completion Once the electrical, mechanical and plumbing were completed upstairs we were able to get our rough inspections and then sheetrock both the upstairs and downstairs at the same time. Our main focus continued to be the upstairs work, including trim, door installation, the bathroom remodeling, and floor repairs, refinishing and paint. Now that the upstairs is almost done, we are shifting our focus back to completing those same phases downstairs after the clients move back in a few weeks. The upstairs will be 100% complete (except for the master bath tile that is taking 4 months to arrive from Italy). What we learned With basement-only projects it is common for our customers to continue living in their homes throughout the job. We were originally hoping our clients could stay at home for the duration, as the remodel initially only involved the bedroom, bath and family room above. But we soon realized that we could accomplish more in a shorter period of time and make changes that would otherwise not be feasible if they moved out. Plus given all the social distancing and protective requirements for isolating the work area due to Covid, that was going to add another layer of complexity to the process of working in the same space as our clients. Our final plan – completing the rough basement first, having our customers move out for the minimum amount of time to complete the upstairs work, and finally finishing the downstairs – became the best approach. The upstairs with the plaster removed. How the design-build approach worked best As design-build contractors, we were able to adapt quickly to make changes. Working directly with our clients to make decisions minimized the need to involve the architect and the City of Oakland’s building department, which have been taking longer than usual to approve plan changes. (see previous articles we wrote about current challenges we’re facing with some East Bay city building departments). Fortunately, most of these decisions were non-structural alterations that didn’t affect the drawings except for a few minor changes the inspector let us defer until the end of the project. And because removing the plaster upstairs sped up our work, and we were able to give the owner a credit back for the wall repairs no longer needed, we achieved a better result in less time for a better price. articles.text: As I walk and look around Piedmont, I suspect that Craftsman homes and their closely related variations make up the most common architectural style in town, in fact, maybe even in the entire Bay Area. The Craftsman, or American Craftsman style of architecture developed to a large degree in tandem with the same style in England. Both are offshoots of the Arts and Crafts movement of the late 19th century, which idealized simplicity, harmony with nature, and honesty in construction. It developed as an alternative to the ornate and opulent style of the Victorian age and indeed resulted in simpler, cleaner and what the architects of the time thought of as a more honest design. Valued and expressed in this architecture was the hand crafting of the building components both on the exterior and interior of the buildings. Even though it may have been largely developed because of nostalgia for the handworked aesthetic of the pre-industrial era, Craftsman buildings were thoughtful and very well constructed by craftspeople who took pride in the quality of their work. Photos by Will Adams Like all good architecture, the inside of a Craftsman home is designed in sympathy with the character of the outside. Here that includes the use of natural materials, fitted exposed beams, wood paneling, and most notably, extensive built-in wood bookshelves, cabinets and window seats. Both Bernard Maybeck and his disciple Julia Morgan are among the famous architects who designed and worked closely with outstanding craftspeople to produce many buildings in this style throughout the East Bay, including a number of homes in Piedmont. Like all styles in the continually evolving field of architecture, there are variations of the American Craftsman genre. These include the Craftsman Bungalow, the Prairie style, and even the Mission Revival style (which we have discussed previously), which according to some historians falls into the Craftsman category, certainly having many of the same characteristics. The development of the Craftsman Prairie style, attributed mainly to Frank Lloyd Wright, is considered by many historians to be the first truly American architectural style! It shares many of the Craftsman characteristics but is generally distinguished and recognizable by a very strong horizontal feeling created by low slope hipped or even flat roofs with even larger overhangs than normal. articles.text: The Fairy Gate at Children’s Fairyland reopened for guests again on March 19, 2021, one year after first being forced to close due to the Covid pandemic. Since reopening, the park has made some changes. Puppeteer Randal Metz now walks through the park instead of putting on large performances on the puppet stage. The 10-acre space is open for business (and fun), including the slides, and nearly 60 storybook sets. Fairyland is operating under Covid red tier restrictions and anxiously awaits entering the orange tier to further unleash the magical world that has dazzled kids since 1950. When orange tier restrictions go into effect, the puppet shows, the Children’s Theater and amusement rides will all be fully open. Fairyland experienced a long delay before it reopened briefly on October 3, 2020, due to its complex status of whether it was an amusement park, historic garden, zoo, or an outdoor museum. It is all four, and eventually had to close again December 7 when the number of COVID cases increased significantly locally and across the entire country. Once Alameda County enters the orange tier, the Jolly Trolly, Alice’s Wonder Go-Round, Anansi’s Web Mini-Ferris Wheel, and the Flecto Carousel can reopen. It will then be classified as an amusement park as opposed to its current designation as an outdoor museum. “Our members really carried us through the pandemic. We received 3,500 donations in three months,” explained Executive Director Kymberly Miller. “They are extraordinary. We are just grateful for them and fully realize how much people really love it here.” Fairyland is currently operating three days a week, Friday through Sunday. Admission is split into two different shifts, morning and afternoon. Tickets may be purchased for either time slot. It is scheduled to move to a five-day schedule (Wednesday through Sunday) on March 31, with plans to return to its seven-day schedule on June 7. Miller has powered through a challenging first year as Executive Director and the place looks clean, bright and cheerful. “Willie the Whale is bright and shiny with a fresh coat of paint, as is our dragon,” said Miller. All indoor features such as the gift shop and member services are outdoors now, and the staff has been increased to meet Covid sanitation requirements. Paths are designated as one way and there is a separate exit now. All the water fountains were upgraded to modern water bottle fillers that turn on with the press of a knee. Masks are required for everyone 3 years old and up. Donations for maintenance, sanitation, and payroll are always welcome during a time of coronavirus. Children’s Fairyland is a non-profit located at Lake Merritt at 699 Bellevue Avenue in Oakland. Hours are Friday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 12 noon, and 1:00 to 4:00 p.m. Purchase tickets online at www.fairyland.org. For questions, call 510-452- 2259. Fairyland visitors enjoyed a little sunshine after the morning rain the day the park reopened. Ryan Gorman (left) and Deborah Wood pose for a photo before Ryan heads down the Dragon Slide.
