articles.text: Piedmont’s native son a world leader of industry, engineering, Scouting and philanthropy Jay Russell Former Piedmont resident and Piedmont High alum Stephen Bechtel Jr. passed away March 15, 2021 in his Pacific Heights apartment in San Francisco. He was 95. Bechtel transformed the family Bechtel construction and engineering company into a global giant with high profile projects including BART, Saudi Arabia’s King Khalid International Airport and work on the Channel Tunnel between Britain and France. Unfettered by fortune and fame, Bechtel never forgot his roots. One of his many philanthropic endeavors, supporting the Piedmont Boy Scout Council, helped it become the top-performing council in the nation. Born Stephen Davison Bechtel Jr. on May 10, 1925 in Oakland, Steve Jr., as he was known, grew up in Piedmont and frequently accompanied his father on inspection trips to Bechtel company projects. One of those projects was the Hoover Dam, 60-stories tall, and considered one of the greatest engineering achievements in history. During Stephen Bechtel, Jr. summers Steve Jr. worked as a sweeper and surveyor’s stake puncher. At an Eagle Scout reunion at the Berkeley City Club in 2010, Bob Coleman, a past president of the Piedmont Scout Council, with tongue in cheek, told the audience that Hoover Dam was actually Mr. Bechtel’s Eagle Scout Project. As a sophomore at Piedmont High, Bechtel became an Eagle Scout. Before graduating from the Piedmont High School Class of 1943 he enlisted in the Marine Corps Reserve. After high school, he initially attended the University of Colorado to study engineering. He later transferred to Purdue University and graduated in 1946 with a Bachelor of Science degree in Civil Engineering. He married Elizabeth Mead Hogan (Betty) the same year. After briefly serving as a Lieutenant in the Marine Corps, he earned a Masters of Business Administration degree at Stanford in 1948. Also in 1948 he officially joined the Bechtel family company. He became its CEO at age 35, and ran the San Francisco-based, global company from [L to R] The Honorable George Schultz, Sam Cardoza, Gideon Cohn-Postar, Wes Motlow, Austin Kelley, Brendan Kelley, Larry Kelley, Stephen Bechtel, and [front center] scouts Will McBain and Connor Christiansen. Stephen Bechtel, Jr. (left) accepts a Giclee copy of a Norman Rockwell painting of the Boy Scouts from Bob Coleman, former President of the Piedmont Scout Council. 1960 to 1990, building major projects throughout the world, including nuclear, security, environmental, oil, gas, chemical and mining. After taking over leadership from his father, he expanded the Bechtel group’s sales 11-fold. Under his leadership as CEO, the Bechtel Group built King Khalid International Airport in Saudi Arabia, Jubail Industrial City in Saudi Arabia, oil platforms in the North Sea, and liquefied natural gas plants in Algeria, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates. Locally, the largest Bechtel construction project was BART, the Bay Area’s first rapid transit system. He was named to presidential or national committees by U.S. Presidents Lyndon B. Johnson, Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford. He retired in 1990 at age 65 and was succeeded as CEO by his son, Riley Bechtel. Stephen Jr’s grandson Brendan Bechtel succeeded Riley in 2016. The company was started by Stephen Jr.’s grandfather, Warren A. Bechtel, in 1898. In the company’s 122- year history, more than 25,000 projects have been completed in 160 countries on all seven continents. But for all the success of the Bechtel Group, he never forgot his hometown and maintained a lifelong involvement with Scouting. In addition to his long list of accomplishments, Bechtel was also a distinguished Eagle Scout from Piedmont’s Troop 4. A lifelong Scout, Bechtel earned his rank of Eagle in 1940. Sixty-five years later, in 2005, he was recognized by the Boy Scouts of America with the Silver Buffalo award for distinguished service to the youth of America. In 2009 the S.D. Bechtel Jr. Foundation made a $50 million donation to the Boy Scouts of America allowed the acquisition of 14,000 acres of land in West Virginia. It was the largest donation in the history of the BSA. The land is now known as the The Summit Bechtel Family National Scout Reserve. “Mr. Bechtel was a champion of Scouting everywhere, but he remained close to Piedmont Scouting,” said former Piedmont Scout Executive Director Jo Hazelett. “He helped the Council in so many ways over the years and he was very kind.” “One memory that stands out is in 2010, when he learned that I had never been to a [National] Jamboree. He insisted on picking up my husband, my dog, and me as we ended a backpacking trip in the Continental Divide in Montana and taking us to the Jamboree in West Virginia on his jet,” said Hazelett. “We had a blast, but it sort of ruined commercial flying for us for a while.” Scouts from throughout the U.S. use The Summit year-round for high adventure and leadership training. It serves as the permanent home for the National Scout Jamboree, a gathering of thousands of members every four years. Stephen Bechtel’s bronze statue at the Summit Bechtel Reserve in West Virginia. Johnson, Richard Nixon and Gerald Ford. He retired in 1990 at age 65 and was succeeded as CEO by his son, Riley Bechtel. Stephen Jr’s grandson Brendan Bechtel succeeded Riley in 2016. The company was started by Stephen Jr.’s grandfather, Warren A. Bechtel, in 1898. In the company’s 122- year history, more than 25,000 projects have been completed in 160 countries on all seven continents. But for all the success of the Bechtel Group, he never forgot his hometown and maintained a lifelong involvement with Scouting. In addition to his long list of accomplishments, Bechtel was also a distinguished Eagle Scout from Piedmont’s Troop 4. A lifelong Scout, Bechtel earned his rank of Eagle in 1940. Sixty-five years later, in 2005, he was recognized by the Boy Scouts of America with the Silver Buffalo award for distinguished service to the youth of America. In 2009 the S.D. Bechtel Jr. Foundation made a $50 million donation to the Boy Scouts of America allowed the acquisition of 14,000 acres of land in West Virginia. It was the largest donation in the history of the BSA. The land is now known as the The Summit Bechtel Family National Scout Reserve. “Mr. Bechtel was a champion of Scouting everywhere, but he remained close to Piedmont Scouting,” said former Piedmont Scout Executive Director Jo Hazelett. “He helped the Council in so many ways over the years and he was very kind.” “One memory that stands out is in 2010, when he learned that I had never been to a [National] Jamboree. For those who missed it, Ms. Singer took issue with the posting of socially progressive signs promoting the best interests of children and minorities, displayed on private property, as “blights” to the City of Piedmont. That someone in our community felt it necessary to scold her fellow Piedmont residents for publicly exercising their constitutionally protected freedom of expression is upsetting. Several other Piedmont community members told me that they were equally appalled by Ms. Singer’s tone-deaf, insensitive comments. I cannot think of a less controversial and less intrusive means of expressing my opinions than posting a modest sized sign in front of my own residence. Piedmonters put up signs on their lawns to show that they care about issues, people, and causes. Our BLM poster says to friends and community members that I am an ally to my black friends, and it publicly acknowledges the pain and hardships of historically marginalized peoples who have been wrongly arrested, prosecuted and convicted or victims of racial profiling or unjustified police violence. Recently Asians in local communities have been violently attacked because people have been brainwashed by racist, ignorant politicians into believing that Asian-Americans are somehow the cause of COVID. I support my fellow Asian community members and thus I have a sign out saying “In This House We Believe” to show support to women, immigrants, black lives and science. As the mother of two schoolaged children, I can attest to the fact that kids are struggling with many aspects of the pandemic. We decided to place a “Open Our Schools” sign in front of our home because the lack of full time in-person educational services in PUSD has been traumatic and challenging for our kids. Supporting the efforts to get kids safely back in school this fall feels right because I believe that in-person learning is best for all our children. Putting comfort and aesthetics above people is the kind of nonsense that gives Piedmont a bad reputation for being elitist. The world is very imperfect right now and there is much that needs to change. Putting up signs to support important causes is just a small step that gives many of us peace and hope of better things to come for the children we are raising in this community. Let’s try to be better and do more. Dr. Tanny Karunakar is an Emergency Physician and mom. A way to make Blair Park suitable for housing Editor: In my opinion, Blair Park is not suitable for housing because it is a north-facing hill with sporadic sunshine. It is a steep hill with little room for gardens in the back, and driveways to each garage would probably mean backing out into Moraga. Instead, I suggest the City consider a plan that includes a centrally located surface parking area for say 8 to 10 cars with turnaround possibility (eliminating the need to back out.) My suggestion includes a continuous sidewalk linking both sides of the parking area with a low fence that prevents small children and off-leash dogs from running onto Moraga Avenue, and a few picnic tables. In my mind, this represents the highest and best use of this lovely green area, now with yellow tulips, for the enjoyment of our citizens. –William Blackwell. articles.text: Sue Smegal has quietly and competently worked behind the scenes of Scouting in Piedmont for decades. For many years, her service on the Piedmont Council’s Executive Board, Advisory Board, and her continuing service on the Eagle Board of Review has upheld the Council’s mission to support youth and families throughout the community. She was an active volunteer supporter of Troop 15 when her son was in Scouts, serving in various unit roles. She’s never sought recognition and has consistently served youth in the community with humility and grace. Considered the consummate event organizer, she was responsible for chairing three major fundraising events for the Scouts. She co-chaired with Allan Dachs a banquet at the Claremont Hotel in 2006 honoring Bob Coleman and celebrating his receiving the Distinguished Eagle Award. In 2010 she chaired an Eagle Scout Celebration honoring 100 years of Scouting in Piedmont. The event was held at the Historic Berkeley City Club. When Bob Coleman introduced Stephen Bechtel, Bob said that Mr. Bechtel’s Eagle Project was building Hoover Dam. (Mr. Bechtel laughed harder than anyone.). In 2014 Sue chaired Roast and a Toast at Golden Gate Fields for Piedmont Post founder Gray Cathrall, a longtime member of the Piedmont Scout Advisory Board. He was presented with the Boy Scouts of America Distinguished Citizen Award. The dinner for Coleman and Cathrall raised significant funds for the Piedmont Council Boy Scouts of America Foundation. Outside of her work with Scouting, Sue served as a middle school teacher for 11 years, followed by eight years as a member of the Piedmont School Board. She recently was recognized with the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award by the Piedmont School District for over 45 years of youth-focused service. She also served with several other nonprofits, including the Ann Martin Center, Hill Branch of Children’s Hospital in Oakland, and the Alameda County Child Abuse Prevention Task Force. She clearly lives the value of “Always Kids First”.
